q1:
I use SQL every day in my current role as a Data Analyst Intern at TikTok Shop UK. I query large merchant and transaction tables to work out what is driving performance across the UK marketplace, for example which groups of merchants are growing, which are falling behind and why. From that analysis I build KPI frameworks and dashboards that the operations, product and commercial teams use to set targets and track the initiatives they are running. I spend a lot of time making sure each metric is defined the same way for everyone and that the data behind it is correct.

I have also used Power BI to build reporting dashboards, and before TikTok I turned research and modelling at Ipsos Strategy3 into dashboards and recommendations for client teams. In my MSc I worked with very large datasets (458,840 UK Biobank participants), which gave me a lot of practice writing clean, reproducible queries and checking data quality before reporting anything.
q2:
I have not worked in insurance yet, but most of my work has been in operational and customer-facing settings. At TikTok Shop UK I sit in the Business Planning & Operations team, and our 'customers' are the merchants selling on the platform. My analysis looks at how they are performing and where they need support, and it feeds into decisions about targets and initiatives across the UK market. That has taught me to look at performance through two lenses at once: the business numbers and what is actually happening to the customer.

Before that, at DS Digital Technology, I worked on a patient-facing service for a pharmaceutical client in a highly regulated healthcare setting. Every output had to meet strict safety standards, so I worked with clinical experts to define exactly what a good outcome looked like and then measured performance against it. I think that is quite close to the kind of customer outcome monitoring that Consumer Duty asks for. At Ipsos Strategy3 I also worked directly on client projects, analysing more than 80 interviews with healthcare professionals to understand their needs.
q3:
At DS Digital Technology, a pharmaceutical client was building an AI assistant to answer questions from patients with bone metastases, but they had no clear way to decide whether an answer was good enough to show a patient. I worked with their clinical experts to turn that into something measurable: 246 realistic patient questions and a scoring rubric across six dimensions, including red-line rules for answers that should never be given. I then built a Python pipeline that tested six different AI models and scored more than 2,400 responses against it.

The outcome was that the client adopted the benchmark as its official acceptance standard, so it directly changed how they decided whether the product was ready. It also showed them clearly where each model was falling short. The main thing I took from it is that agreeing what 'good' looks like with the people who own the problem is the most important step, before building any report or model.
q4:
At TikTok Shop UK I present findings to operations, product and commercial colleagues who do not work with data every day. I have learned to lead with the answer and what it means for them, and keep the technical detail in the background for anyone who wants it.

A good example was when my supervisor asked me to set up a campaign configuration for a list of merchants by hand. After a few examples I could see the logic, so I suggested using Claude Code to build an AI agent to do it, with a validation step to check accuracy. My supervisor was sceptical at first, which was fair, because a wrong setting would affect real merchants. I kept my explanation focused on what the agent would do and how the validation step would check its output, rather than on how it was built, and I delivered it before the same-day deadline. It cut the time the task took by around 40 to 50 percent.

I did something similar in my MSc dissertation, where I turned complex cardiovascular risk models into a simple interactive Streamlit tool so non-specialists could explore the results themselves.
